title: Power Rankings, Week 2: A Whale Sinks, a Doc Rises, and the Weekly Job Admits It Missed a Deadline
dek: This was supposed to run on Oct 13. It didn’t, because the weekly job stalled, so this edition covers the quiet week and the weekend that actually mattered.
intro: Quick confession: this post should have gone up on Tuesday, Oct 13, and it didn’t. The automatic weekly job started and then stopped without writing anything. On Oct 13 Vulture’s official leaderboard still had every team in our league at 0, and the real news came this weekend, so I’m treating this as the Week 2 edition and covering both.

The headline is that the league’s first points arrived on Oct 16–18, from two films. You Can See Everything opened to an estimated $15M from 855 theaters, the best per-theater average among the top eight films, and Whalefall opened to about $7–8M against a roughly $60M budget. Six teams own the doc and one owns the whale. Our live standings below are based on weekend estimates and Vulture’s official board won’t reflect any of it until its next update, so expect small differences.

Same caveat as last week: the projected numbers are my own rough guesses (the film-by-film estimates are saved in the repo now), and the top eight teams are within a few hundred points of each other, so a single Oscar nomination can reorder the whole thing.

rankings.take: Still on top, and it got there by skipping the movie in its name. The team picked a Best Picture roster instead of a whale, which turned out to be the right call: Whalefall opened to about $7–8M on a roughly $60M budget. Meanwhile it owns You Can See Everything, which just opened to $15M, plus Dune, La Bola Negra and Wild Horse Nine. Nothing about this ranking has changed except that the lead got a little more comfortable.

The truth is out, and it’s a B CinemaScore. This team is the only one with Whalefall, and it also owns You Can See Everything, so it leads our live standings with about 23 points (15 + 8). I moved it up one spot because of that doc, not the whale. Avengers: Doomsday (Dec 18) is still the real prize, and the Dec 18 clash with Dune still stands. At least a truther knows how to handle bad news.

A big mover this week, and it’s one film’s doing. You Can See Everything (Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes film, A24) opened to about $15M from just 855 theaters, which looks great for a doc, and this team owns it alongside Dune and La Bola Negra. Having it on the roster also keeps the awards-bro build from looking too precious. I Play Rocky is the one to watch on Nov 13 (limited) and Nov 20.

Up two spots on the same doc. It owns The Odyssey, La Bola Negra, Hunger Games and You Can See Everything, which is a better core than the name suggests. The pun was the best thing about this team last week, and now it has a few points too. It still has no Dune or Avengers, so the ceiling is a bit lower than the top three.
films: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

rankings.take: Down one, and it’s the only team in the top five with nothing on the board. Fjord is its best shot at early points: it opened Oct 9 in four theaters for roughly $124–128K, a good arthouse number but nowhere near the 1 point per $1M the scoring rewards. The roster still has Dune, Hunger Games, La Bola Negra and Tender Loving Care. The waste part of the name is still Coyote vs. ACME and Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie.
films: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

rankings.take: This is the big faller, from 2 to 6, and it’s mostly relative: I raised my estimate for You Can See Everything, which DuneOrDie doesn’t own, so six other teams moved up past it without it doing anything wrong. The whole top eight is within about 400 points, so don’t panic. The name still says Dune or die, and nothing happens until Hunger Games on Nov 20 and Dune on Dec 18. Until then the roster is a lot of waiting.
films: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

rankings.team: Odyssey a lot of movies this year
rankings.take: Up one thanks to You Can See Everything. The pun is still doing most of the work, but the doc gave it 15 real points and La Bola Negra just had a record-setting Netflix opening weekend in four theaters ($277,500, about $69K per theater). This roster has no tentpole, so it’s still an awards-season build, and it has five more months of waiting at the same pace.

Down one and still at zero. The name is a lot to say out loud, and so far the roster has been just as quiet. Wildwood (Oct 23) is its first chance to score, then Wild Horse Nine (Nov 6) and Hunger Games (Nov 20). No You Can See Everything and no La Bola Negra means it avoids the crowd but also missed the one hit of the week.
films: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

rankings.take: No change, and no points. Klara and the Sun opens Oct 23 and Avengers is still the one thing that could change this team’s fortunes. Hexed and Madden are still unconfirmed on my end. It owns La Bola Negra, so it enjoyed the Netflix record without a single point to show for it. The name reads like a password someone made at 2 a.m., and the roster is as chaotic as ever.

Up 15 points and still stuck at 10. You Can See Everything gave pickles69 its first points, which helps, but Coyote vs. ACME, Moana and The Sheep Detectives still can’t earn any box-office points because they opened before Oct 2. The Odyssey and Dune are still a strong core. The 69 is still not helping.
films: Once Upon a Time in Harlem

rankings.take: Still last, still at zero. Fjord opened in four theaters for roughly $124–128K, and Romania selected it as its Oscar submission, which improves the International Feature path. The rest is Obsession and I Want Your Sex, which are locked out of box-office points, and Iron Boy, Josephine and Poetic License. A first team that’s mostly a first draft.

sections.heading: You Can See Everything is the surprise of the weekend
body: A24’s doc about Elizabeth Holmes, from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, opened to roughly $15M from 855 theaters, which is 15 points on its own under the $1M-equals-1-point rule, and a $25M total would add a 10-point bonus. It’s on six rosters (whalefall 4 best picture, whalefall truther, ehootstein, you odyssey that movie, Odyssey a lot of movies this year and pickles69), so it mostly lifts the same teams together. That’s why I raised my estimate for it from about 130 to about 250. I don’t know how its reviews or Letterboxd rating will land, and I’m treating the awards upside (a Best Documentary nomination is worth 25) as a guess.

sections.heading: Whalefall sank
body: Whalefall opened to about $7–8M depending on the source (Box Office Mojo’s estimate is $8.0M), well below the low double-digit projection the studio was reported to be aiming for, with a B CinemaScore. Reviews are middling: reports put its Metacritic score at 62–64, which would be worth 20 points if it holds until Jan 4, and Rotten Tomatoes at roughly 71–79%. I cut my estimate for it from 105 to 70. Only whalefall truther owns it, so the damage is limited to one roster.

sections.heading: La Bola Negra just made Netflix box-office history
body: La Bola Negra opened Oct 16 in four theaters and earned an estimated $277,500, about $69K per theater, and Netflix reported the figure publicly for the first time. Four theaters prove very little about how it plays at scale, and the film reaches Netflix on Dec 2 after a planned 45-day theatrical window, so I don’t expect big box-office points. The awards story is stronger: it’s Spain’s Oscar submission for International Feature, it shared the directing prize at Cannes and won the audience award at TIFF. It’s on 7 of 11 rosters, so it won’t change the order much, and I nudged my estimate up from 400 to about 430.

sections.heading: Fjord and the arthouse numbers
body: Fjord opened Oct 9 in four theaters for roughly $124–128K (sources differ slightly), which is a strong arthouse start but only worth a point or two. Romania selected it as its Oscar submission, which strengthens its International Feature case, so I nudged it from 260 to 280. Two teams own it (waste49 and league first team).

sections.heading: What to watch next
body: Oct 20: Vulture’s next leaderboard update and the next regular power rankings. Oct 23: Wildwood and Klara and the Sun open. Oct 27: Gotham nominations, the first awards points of the season (10–15 points per category). Nov 6: Wild Horse Nine. Nov 13 and 20: I Play Rocky, and Hunger Games on Nov 20.

title: Power Rankings, Week 1: Eleven Teams, Zero Points, Infinite Confidence
dek: Nobody in this league has scored a point, so naturally I’m going to judge everyone.
intro: Verity and Digger are the only films that have scored in the MFL so far, and none of our 11 rosters drafted either one. So the official leaderboard has all of us tied at 0, which means every one of you is currently first place and also last place. Enjoy it. It’s the last time that will be true.

These power rankings are not the standings. They rank each roster by where I expect it to finish after the Oscars, combining each film’s release date and slot, how the festival and awards chatter looks, and how the scoring rules treat it. I didn’t have the draft prices or a preseason ranking to work from, so this edition is the baseline. From next week every team gets a movement arrow against it, and I’ll say whether the change comes from last week’s box office, a shift in awards buzz, or a release date moving.

One caution before the rankings: the point estimates are my own rough guesses, rounded to the nearest 50, and I’m least sure about the small films. The top five are bunched within about 200 points of each other, and a single Best Picture nomination is worth 50. Treat the order as a lean, not a verdict.

rankings.take: A team named after a 2026 movie and a Best Picture wish, and annoyingly, the roster backs it up. This is the only team holding Wild Horse Nine, La Bola Negra and Dune: Part Three, a trio of Oscar-nominee locks (Wild Horse Nine, Martin McDonagh, Searchlight, Nov 6, is being called a sure-fire nominee). Jumanji: Open World (Dec 11) gives it a box-office floor most art-house-heavy teams lack. The only blemishes are NAZA and Wicker, two slots that are essentially paying rent. Whalefall, you’ve been outvoted: this team picked the Oscars instead.

The name says Dune or die, and the roster takes it seriously: Dune: Part Three and The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (Nov 20) give it a box-office core shared only with waste49. Unlike waste49, it skips La Bola Negra (on 7 of 11 rosters), so it gains on everyone if that film stumbles. Godzilla Minus Zero is the sleeper, since its predecessor won the Visual Effects Oscar and a win is 50 points. Klara and the Sun, Ray Gunn, Tangles and Ramayana are lottery tickets, but at least the ticket stubs are unique.
films: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

rankings.take: A truther who is right to believe in this roster. Avengers: Doomsday (Dec 18) is a giant box-office swing only one other team has, and Wild Horse Nine and La Bola Negra give it awards depth. The Whalefall pick opens Oct 16 and will probably be the first film on this roster to score, so the truth is finally coming out, albeit modestly. The danger is Dec 18, when Avengers opens the same day as Dune and the two split the audience and the #1 weekend. Conspiracy theorists love a coincidence like that.

The name tells you the managing style: waste49 has the same energy as someone who found a Hunger Games bracket and committed. The core is strong, with Dune, Hunger Games, La Bola Negra, Fjord (Palme d’Or winner, opens Oct 9) and Tender Loving Care (Mike Leigh). Then the waste kicks in. Coyote vs. ACME and Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie opened before Oct 2, so neither can earn a single box-office point, and Hershey is a mystery. That’s three slots that could be a nice melted-chocolate metaphor.
films: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

rankings.take: A roster for people who say they ‘just love cinema’ and then check the Letterboxd ratings. Dune, La Bola Negra, I Play Rocky (Nov 20, Peter Farrelly’s making-of-Rocky film, a Toronto crowd-pleaser) and Fatherland make a pure awards-season build. One tentpole, no Avengers, no Hunger Games, so it will trail on box office, but it should score steadily from the late-November precursors. Solid floor, lower ceiling, a lot of film-bro energy.

The name is a pun, and the roster is a very good core: The Odyssey, La Bola Negra and Hunger Games. The Odyssey will bank real points from critics, audience and awards, but not from box office (more on that below). Club Kid, The Invite and Iron Boy are mid-tier filler that will need to carry some weight. Capped by having no Dune or Avengers, so this team is an odyssey to somewhere decent but not great.
films: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping
Once Upon a Time in Harlem

rankings.take: The longest name in the league, and the roster is the opposite: it’s tight. The Odyssey, Wild Horse Nine and Hunger Games, with no La Bola Negra, which is a quiet advantage if that film stumbles. Wildwood (Oct 23) is the only other film with real upside. This team is one good Oscar morning away from the top four and one bad one from the bottom. Prosciutto jamón, mamma mia, the ham is thinly sliced.
films: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping

rankings.team: Odyssey a lot of movies this year
rankings.take: The pun is doing a lot of work here. This is an awards-heavy roster (The Odyssey, La Bola Negra, I Play Rocky, Once Upon a Time in Harlem, You Can See Everything) with no tentpole at all. I’d expect a slow start and a late climb that depends entirely on the Oscars, which is a bold way to spend the next five months at zero. The Debut (Dec 11 limited, Dec 25 wide) is the only film with any box-office angle, and it’s a ‘goofy musical’ from Jesse Eisenberg.
films: Once Upon a Time in Harlem

rankings.take: The name sounds like a password someone made at 2 a.m., and the roster is similarly chaotic. Avengers: Doomsday and La Bola Negra are strong anchors, but Hexed and Madden are late-year swings I couldn’t confirm release details for, and Klara and the Sun (Oct 23) and Blue Heron are small films. If Avengers wins its Dec 18 weekend, this team climbs a few spots. If not, it stays here, wondering why it didn’t change its password.

The Odyssey and Dune is the best two-film core outside the top three, and then pickles69 stopped trying. Coyote vs. ACME, Moana and The Sheep Detectives all opened before Oct 2, so they can only score from critics, audience and awards, not box office. That’s three slots with a lower ceiling. This team is in a real pickle, and the 69 does not make it better.
films: Once Upon a Time in Harlem

rankings.take: The name suggests a team that’s still on its first draft, and the roster agrees. The Odyssey, Fjord and I Play Rocky are real assets, but everything else is thin: Obsession and I Want Your Sex opened before Oct 2 and have no box-office path, and Iron Boy, Josephine and Poetic License are long shots. There’s no tentpole and no La Bola Negra or Wild Horse Nine. It needs Fjord to overperform at the Oscars, which is a lot to ask of a first team that’s mostly a first draft.

sections.heading: The La Bola Negra problem
body: La Bola Negra is on 7 of the 11 rosters. You Can See Everything and Once Upon a Time in Harlem are on 6 each, The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three on 5, and Wild Horse Nine and Hunger Games on 4. When a film is on that many rosters, its results move almost everyone together and barely change the order.

So the race will be decided by the films that fewer teams own: Avengers: Doomsday (2 teams), Fjord (2), I Play Rocky (3), Godzilla Minus Zero and Whalefall (1 each) and Jumanji: Open World (1). That’s why teams with fewer overlapping picks, like DuneOrDie and whalefall truther, rank higher than the raw film quality suggests.

sections.heading: The Odyssey is the best film and a bad box-office pick
body: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey opened July 17 and has earned about $620M domestically, but the MFL only awards box-office points for films released on or after Oct 2, so none of that counts. Its value is everything else: it’s the de facto Best Picture frontrunner, it opened to a 4.4 Letterboxd average and a 96% Rotten Tomatoes score, and a Letterboxd average of 4.0 or higher on March 1 is worth 100 points. I couldn’t confirm its Metascore, which is worth up to 100 on Jan 4. Five teams own it. It’s a very good pick, but its ceiling is capped because it can never earn the box-office points that Dune or Avengers can.

sections.heading: The Dec 18 collision
body: Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three both open on Dec 18. That helps no one on the box-office side, because the two will split the biggest weekend of the year and only one can take the #1 spot (worth 20 points for each week at #1). It’s the single biggest swing for whalefall truther (Avengers) and DuneOrDie and the others who own Dune. Hunger Games (Nov 20) has the holiday corridor to itself for about three weeks, and Jumanji (Dec 11) is the next challenger. I’d guess Hunger Games holds #1 for at least two weekends, but that’s a guess, and it depends on how well it opens.

sections.heading: Watch this week and next
body: Oct 9: Fjord opens in limited release, the first of our films to start earning box-office points. Oct 16: Whalefall opens wide, and La Bola Negra and Once Upon a Time in Harlem open in limited release (La Bola Negra reaches Netflix on Dec 2). Oct 23: Wildwood and Klara and the Sun. Oct 27: the Gotham nominations, the first awards points of the season (up to 15 points per category). Nov 6: Wild Horse Nine opens. The first team to leave 0 will probably be whichever one owns Fjord or Whalefall.
